sections.title: Plural nouns
sections.content:
Some nouns are usually plural and take a plural verb:
• The company's earnings have increased for the last five years.
Also: belongings, clothes, congratulations, goods, outskirts, overheads, particulars (= information), premises (= building), riches, savings, stairs, surroundings, thanks
Note that whereabouts can be used with either a singular or plural verb, police and people always take a plural verb, and staff usually does:
• Police believe that Thomas is in Brazil, although his exact whereabouts are / is unknown.
• Staff say that the new computer system has led to greater levels of stress in their work.

sections.title: Plural nouns used with singular verbs
sections.content:
Although the words data and media (= newspaper, television, etc.) are plural (singular datum and medium), they are commonly used with a singular verb. However, in formal contexts such as academic writing a plural verb is preferred. Note that other similar plurals such as criteria and phenomena (singular criterion and phenomenon) are always used with plural verbs. Compare:
• All the data is available for public inspection. (or ... are available ...)
• I agree that the criteria are not of equal importance. (not ... the criteria is not ...)

sections.title: Uncountable nouns ending in -s
sections.content:
Some uncountable nouns always end in -s and look as if they are plural, but when we use them as the subject they have a singular verb:
• The news from the Middle East seems very encouraging.
Also: means (= 'method' or 'money'); economics, linguistics, mathematics, phonetics, physics; politics, statistics, etc. (= academic subjects); athletics, gymnastics; diabetes, measles, rabies.
However, compare:
• academic subject (singular verb): Politics is popular at this university.
• general use (plural verb): Her politics are bordering on the fascist. (= political belief)
• Statistics was always my worst subject. (academic) / Statistics are able to prove anything you want them to. (numerical information)
• Economics has only recently been recognised as a scientific study. (academic) / The economics behind their policies are unreasonable. (the financial system)

sections.title: Agreement with measurements, percentages, etc.
sections.content:
With a phrase referring to a measurement, amount or quantity we usually prefer a singular verb:
• Only three metres separates the runners in first and second places. (rather than ... separate ...)
A singular verb must be used when the complement is a singular noun phrase (e.g. a long time):
• Three hours seems a long time to take on the homework. (not Three hours seem ...)
When the first noun in a complex subject is a percentage or a fraction the verb agrees with the noun closest to the verb. Compare:
• An inflation rate of only 2% makes a difference to exports. (verb agrees with main noun)
• About 50% / half of the houses need major repairs. (verb agrees with closest noun)
Where we use a singular noun that can be thought of as either a whole unit or a collection of individuals, we can use either a singular or plural verb:
• Some 80% of the electorate is expected to vote. (or ... are expected ...)

exercises.question: Dr Darsee's present whereabouts ___ unknown.
exercises.hint: Whereabouts can be used with a singular or plural verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: both 'is' and 'are'
Whereabouts can be used with a singular or plural verb.

exercises.sentence: Either the director or the producers has approved this version of the script.
exercises.correction: Either the director or the producers have approved this version of the script.
exercises.hint: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearest subject. 'Producers' (plural) is nearest.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: the producers have approved
With correlative conjunctions (either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also), the verb agrees with the NEAREST subject (proximity rule). Here, 'producers' is nearest and is plural, so use 'have'. If the order were reversed: 'Either the producers or the director has approved...'

exercises.question: Phenomena such as sun spots ___ puzzled scientists for centuries.
exercises.hint: 'Phenomena' is the plural of 'phenomenon' and takes a plural verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have
'Phenomena' is the plural of 'phenomenon' and takes a plural verb.

exercises.sentence: The committee have reached a decision and will announce it tomorrow.
exercises.correction: The committee have reached a decision and will announce it tomorrow.
acceptable: The committee have reached a decision and will announce it tomorrow.
exercises.hint: 'Committee' in British English = collective noun, can take singular or plural verb depending on meaning.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The committee have reached — CORRECT (British English)
In British English, collective nouns (committee, government, team, staff, audience) can take either singular or plural verbs. Plural is used when the members are acting individually or as separate people; singular when they act as a unit. Both are acceptable — consistency within a text matters most.

exercises.question: Modern linguistics ___ often said to have begun at the start of the 20th century.
exercises.hint: 'Linguistics' refers to an academic subject, so it takes a singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is
'Linguistics' refers to an academic subject, so it takes a singular verb.

exercises.question: Statistics ___ (be) a subject that many students find intimidating.
exercises.hint: Academic subjects ending in -s (statistics, economics, physics) take singular verbs.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is
Academic subjects, fields, and disciplines that end in -s are grammatically singular: statistics is, mathematics is, physics is, economics is, linguistics is. These look plural but are treated as single disciplines. Compare: 'The statistics show...' (= the data = plural) vs 'Statistics is...' (= the subject).

exercises.question: Contact us by whatever means ___ most convenient for you: phone, email or text.
exercises.hint: In this context ('phone, email or text'), 'means' refers to multiple methods, so it takes a plural verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are
In this context ('phone, email or text'), 'means' refers to multiple methods, so it takes a plural verb.

exercises.question: On average, 25 litres of water ___ (be) used each day per household.
exercises.hint: A phrase referring to an amount or quantity usually takes a singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is
A phrase referring to an amount or quantity usually takes a singular verb.
